messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
It’s not uncommon to generate thousands of files during a bioinformatics analysis. In this lesson, we will cover project organization strategies for keeping track of the files we generate, including ways to manage failed software runs and navigating repeat analyses with changing parameters. Be kind to future you: a little organization effort now can save hours of headache later!

Time: 3:10pm-5:00pm
Location: CCAH, Bennett Conference room (http://campusmap.ucdavis.edu/?b=33).

Description

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a community focused on tackling biological big data questions ranging from high level concepts (what is metagenome assembly?) to low level coding problems (what does this error message even mean!?) and everything in between. Each week will start with a short lesson to share important tools for project management and data analysis designed to help us level up our skills. Then, participants with expertise in a variety of areas will be available to help with individual research and coding questions. To facilitate this discussion, all questions must be posted on the MAD discourse forum <https://mad.oxli.org/>. Help us help you: please try to post your questions ahead of time, and be kind to our helpers as they try to get to all the questions! To keep things fun for everyone, please check out our Code of Conduct <http://ivory.idyll.org/lab/coc.html>.

messages.subject: working group 11/14, 11am
messages.body_plain:
Hello D-RUG,

We will have a working group and presentation on Thursday, 11/14 from 11am-1pm. For the part of the session, Will Hemstrom will give an introduction to R package writing and organization. He describes what he will cover below.

R package writing and organization
I used to have an R script. It was a big script, and it represented months of code. Function, followed by function, followed by function. Then, I made a mistake. I came back two months later and tried to figure out what one of those functions did. Big mistake. Clearly, the coder who wrote that function was a moron who didn't bother to document anything. I sighed, sourced, and spent an hour trying to figure out how to use my own code. Then, I looked for a solution.

A big part of what makes R a useful data analysis environment is the availability of a huge range of packages that allow for the use of an immense variety of different methods and data types. Writing your own R package allows you to integrate function documentation into R's help utilities (tab completion! help() functions!), organize your code, and share easy-to-use sets of tools with others or with your grateful future self. In this presentation, we'll go over package creation, structure, and organization. Basic knowledge of function writing is useful but not required!

Please come with the devtools, usethis, and roxygen 2 packages installed! On windows, this will require Rtools; on mac, this will require Xcode; on Linux, this will require black magic (you'll have to google your particular distribution for help).

Additionally, I'm including the schedule for the rest of the quarter for D-RUG below. We'll be picking back up with tidyverse lessons next quarter.

messages.subject: rOpenSci Community Call - Last Night, Testing Saved my Life
messages.subject_clean: rOpenSci Community Call - Last Night, Testing Saved my Life
messages.body_plain:
Hi D-RUG,

Following up on a great presentation by Will Hemstrom today on writing packages in R, here is a community call for rOpenSci on testing from Stefanie Butland, the rOpenSci Community Manager.

All are welcome to join rOpenSci's Community Call on testing in R package development
Thursday, December 5th, 2019; no RSVP needed. 2 speakers & 20 mins for Q&A

Event Details: https://ropensci.org/blog/2019/11/12/commcall-dec2019/
Tweet to share: https://twitter.com/rOpenSci/status/1194646101736882182

Description
As someone with a background in science, not software engineering, Steffi LaZerte will share her experiences using automated testing in R to ensure that packages do what they’re supposed to do, on all the operating systems they’re supposed to do it on, and that they handle weird stuff gracefully.

Rich FitzJohn will talk about how to make testing much more useful than a chore that one does just because it is “best practice”, focussing on how testing has been useful in his work - refactoring code bases, preventing regressions, and improving how code is written in the first place. He will discuss how testing can help at the heart of processes, particularly in collaborative work, and how automating your testing leaves you with more time and energy to focus on your software, and describe strategies for testing as systems grow more complex, such as using mocking to simulate components.

Speaker bios, how to join the call: https://ropensci.org/blog/2019/11/12/commcall-dec2019/.

What’s your story?
What motivated you to start testing?
What do you wish your past-self knew?

messages.subject_clean: Help with if_else inside of group_by?
messages.body_plain:
Hey folks,

I can't figure this one out. Tried the googles and a bunch of random attempts, but I am stumped.

I want to use an if_else statement inside of a group_by inside of a function. I have to filter a big dataset a bunch of times to get plant records from it. Sometimes I want to group the data using the full binomial and sometimes I want to group it by genus only. However, I'm running into a problem in the if_else statement. I suspect the problem is that it's returning the values inside of the column instead of saying "use this column as the grouping variable". I tried using paste() and quoting the column names but that didn't help. I'm guessing there's probably a simple fix, but I haven't been able to figure out the correct things to google.

Here's an example using mtcars:

test_fcn <- function(df, rank){

  df %>%
    group_by(if_else(rank == "yeah", gear, carb)) %>%
    summarise(n = n())

}

test_fcn(mtcars, rank = "yeah")

Error message:
Error: `true` must be length 1 (length of `condition`), not 32

So here, if I say the rank is "yeah" then I want to group_by gear, but if I don't say "yeah" then I want to group by carb (FWIW, in my actual data this is rank = "binom" or "genus", and then I want to use the full binomial or the genus to group by). This works fine when I just remove the if_else and use the column name itself as the argument...but the column names are from this giant database and I don't want to rename the columns.

Any help appreciated.

Thank you!!

John

--
John M. Mola
johnmola.com <http://johnmola.com>

messages.body_plain:
Hello D-RUG!

We will be hosting a Data Carpentry R workshop using the Ecology curriculum. If you're interested in taking it, please submit an application at the link below! We aim to meet the needs of a broad group of people across campus and in the community, so we implemented an application that asks for department/lab affiliation.

Please apply here, details also below! https://registration.genomecenter.ucdavis.edu/events/datalab-data-carpentry-workshop-2019/

Data Carpentry Workshop with R
Dec. 7, 2019, 10 a.m. - Dec. 8, 2019, 6 p.m.
Contact - Please email krli...@ucdavis.edu or tere...@ucdavis.edu if you have any questions.
Location - DataLab Classroom (Shields Library room 360). Directions <http://datalab.ucdavis.edu/directions/>

Data Carpentry develops and teaches workshops on the fundamental data skills needed to conduct research. Its target audience is researchers who have little to no prior computational experience, and its lessons are domain specific, building on learners' existing knowledge to enable them to quickly apply skills learned to their own research. Participants will be encouraged to help one another and to apply what they have learned to their own research problems. We will be covering the Data Carpentry Ecology lessons because they are generally applicable to researchers who aim to do data analysis in R. We will cover data management and organization, manipulating, summarizing, and plotting data in R. For more information, please visit our workshop website. <https://ngs-docs.github.io/2019-12-07-ucdavis-R/>

Who: The course is aimed at graduate students and other academic researchers.

You don't need to have any previous knowledge of the tools that will be presented at the workshop.

Learners must attend both workshop days (Dec 7-8, 2019 from 10am - 6pm each day).

Cost: $10. If the registration fee is a hardship please contact krli...@ucdavis.edu or tere...@ucdavis.edu as limited financial aid is available.

Application deadline is 22 November 2019 at 5pm. Acceptance notices will be sent on 26 November 2019. Accepted individuals have until 2 December 2019 to register, after which their spot will be given to individuals on the waitlist and they will no longer be able to register.

Requirements: Participants must bring a laptop with a Mac, Linux, or Windows operating system (not a tablet, Chromebook, etc.) that they have administrative privileges on. They should have a few specific software packages installed (listed below).

Code of Conduct: Everyone who participates in Carpentries activities is required to conform to the Code of Conduct. <https://docs.carpentries.org/topic_folders/policies/code-of-conduct.html> This document also outlines how to report an incident if needed <https://docs.carpentries.org/topic_folders/policies/code-of-conduct.html>

Accessibility: We are committed to making this workshop accessible to everybody. The workshop organizers have checked that:

         The room is wheelchair / scooter accessible.
         Accessible restrooms are available.

Materials will be provided in advance of the workshop and large-print handouts are available if needed by notifying the organizers in advance. If we can help making learning easier for you (e.g. sign-language interpreters, lactation facilities) please get in touch(using contact details below) and we will attempt to provide them.

Registration closes on: Nov. 22, 2019

Best,
Taylor

Hi John

If you are still interested in  and if anyone has another way of nesting the if_else inside of the group by, I would still like to learn that but otherwise Michael's solution gets the job done.  you can use group_by_at with characters,

group_by_at(if_else(rank == "yeah", "gear", "carb"))
or if you want something more sophisticated (will allow you to use tidyselect machinery) use vars() as below:

library(tidyverse)
test_fcn <- function(df, rank){

  df %>%
    group_by_at(if(rank == "yeah") vars(gear) else vars(carb)) %>%
    summarise(n = n())

}

test_fcn(mtcars, rank = "yeah")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>    gear     n
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     3    15
#> 2     4    12
#> 3     5     5
test_fcn(mtcars, rank = "not yeah")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>    carb     n
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     7
#> 2     2    10
#> 3     3     3
#> 4     4    10

messages.body_plain:
Just a note —

I would *highly* recommend not doing this:

if (x == T) {
 stuff()
}

This is a well-known bad practice in R; unlike the reserved keyword TRUE, T is a variable that can be assigned non-TRUE values. This leads to incredible difficult to debug issues when someone in upstream code assigns T <- 0 or something, e.g.

> T <- 0
> x <- TRUE
> if (x == T) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
[1] "x is evaluating to FALSE"
> if (x == TRUE) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
[1] "x is evaluating to TRUE "

The best way to do this is to just write:

> if (x) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
[1] "x is evaluating to TRUE "

since x is a logical.

Vince

messages.body_plain:
While we’re talking about best practices for control statements in R, == is vectorized (it returns an object with the length of its longest input), but if() and other control statements only expect a single value.  Plus == propagates NAs:

> NA == NA
[1] NA

Which can cause errors or unexpected behavior:

> if (NA == NA) print('foo')
Error in if (NA == NA) print("foo") :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

For a comparison in a control statement, use identical().  It always returns a single value, treats NA as identical to NA, and takes arguments allowing you to specify assumptions, e.g., whether you care about attributes.

> if (identical(NA, NA)) print('foo')
[1] “foo"

If you’re comparing numerics and you want to tolerate some small differences, you can use isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)).  Check out the help on all.equal() for more.

Dan

> }
>

>
> > T <- 0
> > x <- TRUE
> > if (x == T) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
> [1] "x is evaluating to FALSE"
> > if (x == TRUE) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
> [1] "x is evaluating to TRUE "
>
> The best way to do this is to just write:
>
> > if (x) { print("x is evaluating to TRUE ") } else { print("x is evaluating to FALSE") }
> [1] "x is evaluating to TRUE "
>
> since x is a logical.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

New sequencing data is really exciting, but most analysis workflows have many steps to get from raw sequencing data to results. Today, we will work to understand what k-mers are and how we can use them to generate quick insights or find contamination from sequencing data ranging from raw RNA-seq reads to genomes and metagenomes.

Time: 3:10pm-5:00pm
Location: CCAH, Bennett Conference room (http://campusmap.ucdavis.edu/?b=33).

Description

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a community focused on tackling biological big data questions ranging from high level concepts (what is metagenome assembly?) to low level coding problems (what does this error message even mean!?) and everything in between. Each week will start with a short lesson to share important tools for project management and data analysis designed to help us level up our skills. Then, participants with expertise in a variety of areas will be available to help with individual research and coding questions. To facilitate this discussion, all questions must be posted on the MAD discourse forum <https://mad.oxli.org/>. Help us help you: please try to post your questions ahead of time, and be kind to our helpers as they try to get to all the questions! To keep things fun for everyone, please check out our Code of Conduct <http://ivory.idyll.org/lab/coc.html>.

27-Nov Thanksgiving – no MAD
4-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 1
11-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 2

More info

https://dib-training.readthedocs.io/en/pub/#meet-and-analyze-data-mad

Best,

Hey all,

I have a complicated SPDF made up of multiple joined geometries that I'm attempting to using for making some maps, and I am getting the following error when trying to create an sf object:

> test <- st_as_sf(dta)
Error in createPolygonsComment(p) :
  rgeos_PolyCreateComment: orphaned hole, cannot find containing polygon for hole at index 24

Roger Bivand suggested the following fix (https://www.mail-archive.com/r-h...@r-project.org/msg140173.html), which also gives an error:

> test2 <- slot(dta, "polygons") <- lapply(slot(dta, "polygons"), checkPolygonsHoles)
Error in rgeos::createPolygonsComment(oobj) :
  rgeos_PolyCreateComment: orphaned hole, cannot find containing polygon for hole at index 219

Any suggestions for finding/fixing this?

The RDS is 67MB so I'm not sure you want to examine the whole thing, but the gdrive link is here: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1X-V-ZeqKeybGevW9xxpLAHUbJhXxLdWY
